headline: Colombia Centralizes the Quake Count
deck: The presidency reports 181 dead, 2,595 injured and 195 missing while regional tallies continue to run ahead. Command is unified; the count is still catching up.
body: Colombia put one national ledger above hundreds of local rescue sites on the earthquake’s second day. President Abelardo de la Espriella’s Pereira briefing counted 181 people dead, 2,595 injured and 195 missing [E1]. The same account listed 1,136 homes destroyed and 8,357 damaged [E1]. Those figures supersede the first-day wire tally reported in this paper, but they do not close the count.

Infrastructure now has its own national inventory. The presidency reported 48 collapsed buildings, 807 damaged education centres, 85 health centres, 74 roads, 16 aqueducts and one runway affected [E1]. Each category converts a geological event into a queue for engineers, beds, classrooms and access. The rubble is counted in people first and in public systems immediately after.

Regional authorities and local media still publish totals that can outrun the presidential figure. They cover overlapping cities and departments, use different update times and may classify missing or transferred patients differently. Adding those lists would produce a larger number and a worse ledger. The national total must be read as an as-of count from the unified command, not as a ceiling on the eventual toll [E1].

Search operations continued in Chocó while the government tried to bring the remote Pacific side of the disaster into the same command picture [E2]. UNGRD described an extraordinary risk-management council with the governor and sent technical teams to assess structures [E2]. Urban rescue in Cali and Pereira can move people and machinery quickly; damaged roads and communications make the epicentral corridor a slower ledger. The operational gap is geography before it is bureaucracy.

Foreign help began arriving in named packages. El Salvador’s president said two cargo aircraft would carry 100 tonnes of requested supplies, without personnel, and Colombia’s president publicly accepted the offer [E3][E4]. That distinction matters because an offered team, a dispatched aircraft and material received at a distribution point are three separate stages. Aid becomes useful only after the last handoff.

Centralising public information can reduce duplicate deaths and contradictory orders. It can also make the official number lag mayors who can see a collapsed block before Bogotá can reconcile the form. The test is whether one reporting channel accelerates food, shelter, medical capacity and road clearance while preserving local detail. A lower national count is not evidence of better conditions; it is evidence of a narrower accounting perimeter.

The response is functioning, but not synchronized. Rescue teams are working, foreign cargo is moving and a damage matrix exists [E1][E2][E3]. Meanwhile, the distance between the presidential ledger and the local lists remains a measure of unfinished access. Colombia has found a single place to print the number. It has not yet reached every place the number comes from.
